opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't really see a contradiction there. I've been doing deep learning for a long time, and I still think it's an incredibly powerful tool. But I've always been clear about what it's good at and what it isn't.

Deep learning is fundamentally about learning continuous geometric transformations from data. You take an input space and map it to an output space through a series of smooth, differentiable steps, and you fit that mapping with gradient descent. That works remarkably well for what I'd call perception-type problems, or more broadly "type one" thinking: pattern recognition, intuition, fast approximate judgment. Anything where you have a dense sampling of the space you care about and where interpolating between training examples gets you the right answer.

But a lot of what we care about in intelligence isn't like that. Reasoning, planning, abstraction, the ability to deal with something genuinely novel, those involve discrete, step-by-step, compositional processing. That's the kind of thing programs are naturally good at, and that curve-fitting is naturally bad at. If you try to encode a sorting algorithm or a simple arithmetic procedure into a neural network, you need enormous amounts of data, you only get an approximation, and it breaks as soon as you go a little outside the training distribution. Whereas a few lines of explicit code generalize perfectly, and that code was much simpler to arrive at.

So my view has always been that the path forward is a hybrid. You want deep learning as the intuition engine and symbolic, program-like structures as the reasoning engine, and they should work together. The really interesting case is using deep learning to guide program search. Discrete program search is extremely powerful but suffers from combinatorial explosion, and what's missing is good intuition about which parts of the search space to explore. That's precisely what deep learning can provide. Humans work the same way. When a chess player looks at a position, they don't enumerate every move. Their intuition narrows it down to two or three candidates, and then they reason explicitly through those.

So it's not that I've turned away from deep learning. It's that I've always seen it as one half of the picture. People sometimes hear me criticize the idea that scaling up deep learning alone will get us to general intelligence, and they take that as being anti-deep-learning. It isn't. It's about using each tool for what it's good at and building systems that combine them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the path forward is a hybrid: deep learning provides intuition while symbolic, program-like structures provide reasoning, and the two work together.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't see it as a contradiction at all. I've never been committed to deep learning as an ideology. I've been committed to it as a tool, and for a long time it was the most powerful tool we had for a very specific class of problems: perception, pattern recognition, anything where you have a lot of data and the task is essentially interpolation on a learned manifold. For that, deep learning is extraordinary, and I still think it's the right answer.

But I've also been saying since roughly 2017, 2018, that deep learning on its own hits a wall when you ask it to do things that are fundamentally about discrete program synthesis. Things like reasoning, abstraction, adapting to a genuinely novel situation that isn't well covered by your training distribution. That's not a bug you fix with more data or more parameters. It's a structural limitation of what a differentiable function approximator is.

So the way I think about it, you have two kinds of abstraction. There's value-centric abstraction, which is what deep learning does beautifully: comparing things by similarity, by distance in some continuous space. That's perception, intuition, pattern matching. And then there's program-centric abstraction, which is about exact structure, about discrete rules that compose, about finding the program that explains a situation. That's what symbolic methods are good at, and it's what discrete search is good at.

Human intelligence very obviously uses both. You have fast intuitive pattern recognition and you have slow, deliberate, step-by-step reasoning, and they feed into each other. So my view is that the path forward is to merge these. Use deep learning to guide program search, to provide the intuition that prunes the search space, and use discrete program synthesis to actually produce the kind of generalization that pure gradient descent can't. That's really what ARC is about for me. It's a benchmark designed so that neither approach alone can crack it.

So from the outside maybe it looks like a pivot. From the inside it's been the same question the whole time: what is intelligence, actually, and what does it take to build it? Deep learning was a big part of the answer. It was never the whole answer.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the path forward is to merge deep learning with symbolic methods, using deep learning to guide program search and discrete synthesis to complement it.

astra-6.text:
I don’t see a contradiction there. My interest has always been in intelligence, and deep learning is a very powerful tool for getting us there. But that doesn’t mean it has to be the only tool.

Deep learning is particularly good at perception, at learning useful representations from messy data. Symbolic approaches give you a way to express things precisely and compose them explicitly. You can take a small set of rules or operations and combine them to solve a problem you haven’t encountered before.

The interesting question is how these capabilities can work together. Could you use deep learning to guide a search over programs, for example? You learn from experience which directions are promising, but the solution you construct is a program that you can execute and reuse.

So, for me, being committed to deep learning doesn’t mean being committed to the idea that scaling one technique will solve every problem. It means understanding what that technique does well and figuring out how to build on it.

r001.rationale: The response says symbolic approaches and deep learning can work together, including using deep learning to guide program search, and describes symbolic methods as a way to build on deep learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t see these as opposing commitments. Deep learning is very good at learning useful representations from data. But learning a representation and reasoning with it are different problems, and I don’t think we should assume that one mechanism has to do everything.

Symbols give you a way to express abstractions explicitly and recombine them. You can take something you already know and use it in a new situation without having to learn that situation from scratch. Of course, the difficult question is where those symbols come from and how they acquire meaning. Simply putting a symbolic system on top of a neural network doesn’t solve that.

What interests me is the interaction: learning representations through experience, then using those representations in a more deliberate process of abstraction, search, and composition. Deep learning can be an important part of that system without being the entire system.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining learned representations with symbolic abstraction, search, and composition, and says deep learning can be an important part of the larger system. This clearly presents symbolic elements as augmenting deep learning.
